strengths: First systematic investigation of Video LLM safety; addresses critical understudied gap with strong motivation
Comprehensive VideoSafetyBench dataset (77.6k samples, 19 subcategories, 10 languages) grounded in real-world policies—valuable community resource
Clear empirical findings demonstrating 42.3% safety degradation with video modality and 65.1% improvement with VideoSafety-R1
Extensive evaluation across 14 model variants and multiple benchmarks with thorough ablation studies and cross-dataset generalization
Well-motivated dual-stage approach combining explicit harm detection (alarm tokens) with reasoning-enhanced defense (Safety-Guided GRPO)
Excellent documentation including annotation pipelines, prompts, hyperparameters, and dataset statistics supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Alarm tokens are simple learnable embeddings; GRPO and multi-task learning are established techniques. Primary contribution is application rather than methodology.

Evaluation methodology heavily relies on LLM-based assessment (Qwen-Long) with small human validation set (114 samples for 11.4k test set); unclear if single-model validation captures systematic biases
Concerning increase in False Refusal Rate from 0.7% to 13.4% (12.7% absolute increase); insufficient discussion of safety-usability tradeoff and deployment implications
VideoSafety-R1 only trained and evaluated on VideoLLaMA3-2B; generalization to other architectures, model scales, or video LLMs unclear despite indirect image-benchmark evidence
Synthetic training data (LLM-generated CoT annotations with templates) lacks comparison to human-written examples; risk of learning template artifacts rather than generalizable reasoning
Dataset construction relies on proprietary APIs for annotation (Qwen-Max-VL, VideoLLaMA3) without inter-annotator agreement metrics; 15-second clips may lose contextual information
Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; unclear stability across random seeds
Limited analysis of failure modes, category-specific underperformance (e.g., Alcohol/Tobacco), or sophistication of semantic attacks explored
No comparison with alternative safety alignment approaches (Constitutional AI, DPO variants, other fine-tuning strategies) beyond base LLM baseline
Proprietary dependencies (Qwen models, GPT-4o for annotation; Qwen-Long for evaluation) limit full reproducibility despite code availability claims

strengths: Addresses timely problem of video LLM safety, an understudied area with clear importance
Large-scale benchmark (VSB-77k) with 77,646 samples across 19 subcategories, 6 principal categories, and 10 languages grounded in real-world policies
Clear empirical finding that video modality degrades safety by average 42.3% (up to 79.4% for VideoLLaMA3-2B), well-documented across multiple models
Comprehensive evaluation across 14 model variants and multiple benchmarks (VSB-Eval, MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep, MVBench, VideoMME, etc.)
Strong empirical gains: 65.1% DSR improvement on VSB-Eval-HH with reasonable cross-benchmark generalization (+59.1% MMBench, +44.3% VLGuard)
Extensive supplementary material including detailed annotation prompts, model descriptions, dataset statistics, and qualitative case studies
weaknesses: Benchmark construction relies heavily on proprietary LLM annotation (Qwen-Max-VL, Qwen-Long, VideoLLaMA3) with insufficient human validation (only 114 samples, 6 per category, 5 annotators, no inter-annotator agreement reported)
Circular annotation concern: using VideoLLaMA3 to re-describe 'presumed harmful' clips to bypass safety censorship introduces potential bias and validity questions for a safety benchmark

Limited technical novelty: AT-SFT is standard multi-task learning; alarm tokens are straightforward learnable embeddings; GRPO adaptation with binary rule-based rewards is incremental; Dynamic Reward Adaptation (Eq. 4) is simple indicator function without sensitivity analysis
High false refusal rate (13.4% on VSB-Eval-SafeQ) inadequately addressed; marginal improvement over text-only baseline (15.7%) raises real-world deployment concerns

Evaluation methodology limitations: binary DSR judgment oversimplifies safety; Qwen-Long evaluation shows only 92.1% accuracy (2nd to Gemini at 93%); no adversarial/adaptive attack evaluation; no failure mode analysis

Severely limited experimental scope: VideoSafety-R1 trained and evaluated only on VideoLLaMA3-2B (small model); generalizability to larger models and architectures unverified; no ablation of hyperparameters (λ₁, λ₂, learning rates)
Data contamination risks from multiple models used in annotation pipeline potentially having overlapping training data

Technical choices unjustified: arbitrary DINOv2 similarity threshold (≥0.5), undefined α_min/α_max bounds, unclear rationale for sample proportions in training stages, no CoT template sensitivity analysis
Benchmark language diversity (10 languages) collected but not analyzed; per-language performance breakdown absent
Reproducibility concerns: reliance on proprietary APIs, complex multi-agent annotation pipeline incompletely documented, no explicit code availability commitment

strengths: Addresses critical gap: First comprehensive study of video LLM safety with large-scale, multilingual benchmark (77k samples, 19 categories, 10 languages) grounded in real-world policies
Significant empirical findings: Demonstrates 42.3% average safety degradation when video modality is integrated and proposes effective mitigation (65.1% improvement on VSB-Eval-HH)
Comprehensive evaluation: Systematic assessment of 14 Video LLM models across multiple evaluation subsets with strong generalization to image safety benchmarks (MMBench +59.1%)

High-quality dataset contribution: Multi-agent annotation pipeline with careful verification, well-balanced category distribution, and extensive documentation will serve as valuable resource for research community
Maintains task performance: Achieves safety improvements while preserving video understanding capabilities (−0.475% average degradation on video benchmarks)
Well-motivated technical approach: Dual-modality verification through alarm tokens and dynamic reward adaptation are intuitive for video-query pairs
Thorough ablation studies: Clear decomposition of component contributions showing complementary roles of AT-SFT and GRPO
weaknesses: Evaluation methodology concerns: Heavy reliance on Qwen-Long as judge for DSR metric with insufficient human validation (only 114 samples with 5 annotators); binary classification is coarse for nuanced safety judgments; no independent verification on substantial test portions
Circular dependency in annotation: Uses AI-generated annotations (from Qwen, VideoLLaMA) that are then evaluated by similar LLMs, raising concerns about data contamination and systematic bias

High false rejection rate: FRR increases from 0.7% to 13.4%, which is problematic for deployment despite being framed as improvement over base LLM (15.7%); no analysis of false refusal patterns or mitigation strategies
Limited method novelty: Alarm tokens are straightforward extensions of existing techniques; GRPO is prior work; main novelty is application to video domain rather than methodological innovation

Questionable dataset quality: All annotations are AI-generated without human ground truth; template-driven query generation may introduce artificial patterns; no inter-rater agreement analysis with humans

Generalization concerns: VideoSafety-R1 trained only on VideoLLaMA3-2B; unclear how well defenses transfer to architectures with different design principles; limited evaluation on models with diverse LLM backbones

Incomplete vulnerability analysis: Section E.2.2 shows video/image vulnerability is comparable (48.3% vs 51.3%), undermining claims about 'unique risks' of video modality; suggests vulnerability stems from semantic complexity rather than temporal structure
Statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; single runs without variance analysis across random seeds; improvements could be within noise margins
Missing baselines: No comparison to adapted image safety methods or simpler prompt-based approaches; Table 5 shows GRPO alone achieves 83.6%, making AT-SFT's necessity unclear

strengths: Comprehensive large-scale benchmark (VideoSafetyEval) with 11.4K video-query pairs across 19 subcategories addressing an important gap in video LLM safety evaluation
Important empirical finding that video modality degrades safety performance by 34.2% on average across models, highlighting unique challenges of video-based LLMs
Extensive evaluation spanning 21 Video LLM variants with multiple safety benchmarks (VSE-HH, VSE-SH, VSE-SafeQ) and systematic ablation studies showing contribution of each component
Rigorous human annotation verification with reported accuracy of 97.44% for queries and 94.84% for video labels, supporting dataset quality
Thorough experimental analysis including cross-lingual performance, cross-dataset generalization, and frame-length analysis with practical insights about semantic harmfulness
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components (alarm tokens, GRPO, chain-of-thought reasoning) are well-established; main contribution is combining existing techniques for video domain rather than methodological innovation

Dataset construction concerns: Harmful videos and queries are automatically generated using LLMs (Qwen-Max) with filtering; no validation that synthetic attacks represent realistic harmful video-query interactions; limited diversity beyond templated patterns

Evaluation methodology issues: Primary reliance on LLM-based evaluation (Qwen-Long) for Defense Success Rate and Helpfulness without sufficient human validation; only limited human verification on sample; no inter-annotator agreement for LLM evaluations; potential circular dependency if training data generated by same models

Inadequate baseline comparisons: Primarily compares against baseline models without defenses rather than state-of-the-art safety methods; limited direct comparison with prior defense mechanisms (Self-Reminder, SPA-VL, MM-RLHF); missing comparison with recent 2024-2025 multimodal alignment work

Generalization concerns: Cross-lingual experiments show trade-offs (better DSR but worse helpfulness in non-English), suggesting language bias; long-video performance degrades (Table 4); cross-dataset generalization only tested on image datasets; unclear generalization to future video LLM architectures

Experimental design issues: Massive jump in performance from Fine-Tuning alone (18.4%) to +Alarm Token (74.0%) in Table 6 suggests potential data leakage or methodology issues not fully explained; limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis beyond Table 15; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Reproducibility limitations: Dataset promised but not currently publicly available; exact LLM prompts for generation/evaluation not fully specified; dependency on closed-source APIs (Alibaba Cloud) makes reproducibility difficult; training details scattered across appendices

Limited failure analysis: Lacks investigation of false positive/negative rates, specific attack types the method is vulnerable to, and when/why the method fails; attention sink analysis (Figure 7) is superficial; no comparison of safety-utility trade-offs at different operating points

Evaluation metrics concerns: Defense Success Rate only measures refusal, not quality or safety of responses; Helpfulness Score is vaguely defined and potentially manipulable; no validation that higher DSR corresponds to improved actual safety; missing nuanced evaluation of borderline cases

Ethical and scope limitations: Limited discussion of potential harms from releasing comprehensive harmful content benchmark; unclear access restriction implementation; does not address emerging threats (adversarial videos, deepfakes); limited to visual-textual modalities; no discussion of misuse potential or defense-evasion attacks

strengths: Addresses critical understudied problem: demonstrates video modality degrades safety performance by ~34.2% across 21 models, exposing systematic vulnerability in Video LLMs
Comprehensive benchmark resource: 11.4k video-query pairs across 19 subcategories, 10 languages, with rigorous multi-agent annotation framework and 97.44% human verification accuracy

Strong empirical validation: systematic evaluation across 21 Video LLM variants, multiple benchmarks (VSE, MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep), cross-lingual testing, and detailed ablations confirming component contributions
Practical defense framework: VideoSafety-R1 achieves 71.1% DSR on VSE-HH with modest generalization trade-offs and maintains utility on general tasks, demonstrating engineering effectiveness

Thorough analysis and insights: frame-count dynamics (Section 5.5), reasoning diversity, per-category breakdowns, semantic richness analysis, and 19 qualitative case studies providing interpretability

Excellent reproducibility: 59-page submission with detailed appendices covering dataset pipeline, training recipes (Appendix G), prompts (Appendix R), hyperparameter settings, and implementation details
Responsible research practices: explicit ethics statement addressing harmful content, privacy protection mechanisms, language bias analysis, and clear data release plans with appropriate safeguards
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (chain-of-thought, token injection, GRPO) are established techniques; contribution is primarily in effective combination rather than algorithmic innovation
Modest generalization: strong improvements on VSE-HH (71.1%) but weaker on other benchmarks (MMBench 44.3%, VLGuard modest gains), suggesting safety alignment may be somewhat dataset-specific

Incomplete attack coverage: focus on relatively simple query-based attacks; more sophisticated attacks (adversarial visual perturbations, semantic manipulations) identified as future work but not explored
Video processing limitations: default 1 FPS sampling may miss harmful content; paper acknowledges safety doesn't consistently improve with longer videos but lacks satisfactory explanation
Training complexity concerns: four-stage pipeline with different optimizers and 15k cold-start samples could limit reproducibility and applicability; end-to-end training time not reported
Insufficient failure analysis: while 19 cases presented, limited investigation of systematic failure patterns or why certain categories (Self-Harm, Platform Information) show lower performance
Dataset edge case handling: 4-5% gap between analysis reliability (99%) and query label agreement (94.84%) indicates difficult consensus cases; inter-annotator agreement statistics not provided
Evaluation metric simplicity: DSR and Helpfulness Score are useful but relatively basic; safety-helpfulness trade-off deserves more thorough exploration
Reasoning data artifacts: VideoSafetyThinking dataset uses Qwen-Max for initial chains with no discussion of potential annotation artifacts or model-specific reasoning patterns
Limited concurrent work comparison: while recent safety benchmarks cited, detailed performance comparisons with concurrent work would better contextualize contributions
